title: Is an embedding layer doing any computation?
motivation: I got stuck on the constructor before reaching the actual model. Was I using an existing embedding layer, or implementing one?
intuition: An embedding is a trainable lookup table. With V tokens and width D, its weight has shape (V, D). Indexing it with token IDs of shape (B, T) produces (B, T, D). It is also equivalent to multiplying one-hot vectors by that table, without constructing the one-hot vectors.
takeaway: The useful distinction is ownership: a custom nn.Module registers its own Parameter; nn.Embedding already does that work. A constructor error says nothing about the quality of the learned representation.

title: Why does Linear(3, 2) store a (2, 3) matrix?
motivation: The argument order and the weight shape looked contradictory when I connected the feed-forward layers.
intuition: The arguments describe a transformation from 3 inputs to 2 outputs. Each output needs three weights, so there are two rows of three weights. With row-vector inputs, forward uses the transpose.
takeaway: Writing out one multiplication was more useful than memorizing the convention. It also made the two expansion projections and the contraction projection in SwiGLU much easier to check.

title: Why does SwiGLU need three matrices?
motivation: The feed-forward block suddenly had two input projections instead of one. I wanted to know what the extra branch was buying.
intuition: Both branches expand D features to F features. One passes through SiLU and gates the other by elementwise multiplication. A third projection maps the resulting F features back to D.
takeaway: The gate is a continuous feature-wise modulation, not a choice of tokens or a miniature attention layer. Thinking of one branch as content and the other as its modulation makes the shape bookkeeping natural.

title: Why are there still two sums in cross-entropy?
motivation: One-hot targets collapse the sum over classes. So why did my implementation still need a vocabulary reduction and a mean over positions?
intuition: The target selects one log probability, but that probability still contains the softmax normalizer over all vocabulary candidates. After computing one loss per position, training averages those losses over the batch and sequence.
takeaway: These reductions answer different questions: how much probability belongs to the correct token, and how to aggregate prediction errors. Keeping the vocabulary axis separate from the position axes prevents a surprising number of bugs.

title: Why is logits[:, targets] the wrong selection?
motivation: I wanted one correct-token score per row. Instead, indexing silently gave me a whole matrix.
intuition: For logits shaped (3, 5) and targets [1, 0, 4], this expression selects all three target columns from every row. The result is (3, 3). The intended coordinates are (0, 1), (1, 0), and (2, 4).
takeaway: The intuition is paired coordinates, not a rectangular slice. Once I drew the three selected cells on paper, advanced indexing stopped looking mysterious.

title: What is keepdim actually keeping?
motivation: The formula was right, but subtracting a per-row maximum either failed or broadcast in the wrong direction.
intuition: Reducing (S, V) over the vocabulary gives (S, 1) with keepdim=True, or (S,) without it. Broadcasting aligns dimensions from the right. The singleton vocabulary axis tells the operation to reuse one number across each row.
takeaway: Equal dimension sizes can hide an incorrect broadcast. A small example with different sequence and vocabulary sizes is a better check than relying on a large tensor that happens to run.

title: Why can a stable softmax still produce log(0)?
motivation: I had already subtracted the maximum. Why was taking the logarithm still unsafe?
intuition: Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow; a sufficiently small probability can still underflow to zero. For logits [0, -1000], the second log probability should be approximately -1000, even if the probability itself cannot be represented.
takeaway: Stay in log space. Computing logsumexp minus the target logit avoids materializing a tiny probability only to take its logarithm. The order of operations matters even when two formulas are algebraically identical.

title: Why is variance the wrong denominator for RMSNorm?
motivation: My outputs were consistently close to the reference, but not close enough. Increasing the tolerance would have hidden the actual mistake.
intuition: RMSNorm uses sqrt(mean(x squared) + epsilon). Variance first subtracts the mean and measures a different quantity. For [2, 2], the RMS is 2 while the variance is zero.
takeaway: Normalization is not one interchangeable operation. The exact statistic, epsilon placement, and accumulation precision are part of the layer definition. Here, I want a scale estimate without centering the vector.

title: Are Adam’s bias correction and normalization the same thing?
motivation: I understood the recursive compression of past gradients. The initialization correction and the second-moment denominator were the parts I kept mixing up.
intuition: The moving averages start at zero, so their early values are biased toward zero. Dividing by 1 minus beta to the power t corrects that effect. With a constant gradient of 2 and beta1=0.9, the first moment is initially 0.2; correction brings it to 2.
takeaway: Dividing the corrected first moment by the square root of the corrected second moment is a separate operation: it scales each coordinate using its own gradient history. It does not normalize the entire gradient vector to unit length.
code:
m_hat = m / (1 - beta1**t)
step = lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps)
reading: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

title: Can a compact residual expression run attention twice?
motivation: I wrote the Transformer block as one long expression, then realized the attention call appeared in two different places.
intuition: Repeated function calls generally mean repeated computation. Compute the attention residual once, store the resulting hidden state, and feed that state to the second normalization and the feed-forward network.
takeaway: This also exposes the pre-norm structure: normalization is inside each residual branch. A short intermediate variable can express the architecture more accurately than an impressive-looking one-liner.
code:
h = x + attention(norm1(x))
y = h + ffn(norm2(h))
reading: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture

title: Is a hidden state really richer than the logits?
motivation: In our discussion of latent communication, I objected that the final hidden state was only one matrix multiplication away from vocabulary scores.
intuition: That objection matters. If the output matrix has full column rank, exact logits can mathematically determine its input vector. The obvious compression occurs when we sample or take argmax and retain only one token.
takeaway: The useful comparison is not simply hidden state versus logits. It is continuous representation versus a selected token, together with the receiving model’s interface, precision, and training objective. A vector is not automatically a useful message.
code: h in R^D -> W_out h in R^V -> one token
reading: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models

title: Does seeing the whole prefix make the last state a summary?
motivation: I was skeptical of treating the final token representation as a complete message about everything that came before it.
intuition: Attention provides a path to earlier positions, not a guarantee that their useful information survives in a single vector. Next-token training rewards predictive representations, which need not preserve every fact a different agent might need.
takeaway: A communication claim needs a receiver-side test: compare text, single-position vectors, and multiple-position representations; remove or shuffle messages. Access to information and a sufficient summary are different capabilities.
reading: Attention Is All You Need — architectural background

title: Why does the first token after switch-off not prove persistence?
motivation: In my steering experiments, the first generated token seemed to retain the intervention. The timing turned out to be crucial.
intuition: The logits at the last prompt position predict the first new token. If steering was active over that prompt position, that prediction still came from steered computation. The next unsteered forward position predicts the second generated token.
takeaway: There is another complication: the first selected token can itself change the future context. Fixed-token scoring and free generation therefore answer different questions. This alignment check came from the experiment; the paper below is background on activation steering.
code:
last prompt position -> token 1
token 1 position -> token 2
reading: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering

title: Does a KV cache belong to the input or the model?
motivation: My adapter experiments kept running into the same question: what exactly becomes stale when the weights change?
intuition: Both determine the cache. Keys and values are projections of hidden states, and those hidden states depend on the prefix and earlier model computations. Keeping the tokens fixed does not guarantee the same cached tensors under different parameters.
takeaway: The useful experiment crosses the current reader with the model that wrote the cache. It separates present parameter effects from historical computation. LoRA provides background on parameter adaptation; it does not itself establish that an old cache can be reused safely.
code:
K_l = H_l W_K,l
V_l = H_l W_V,l
reading: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

title: What do tied embeddings actually share?
motivation: Using the embedding transpose as the output projection looks almost too simple. I wanted to pin down what changes in training.
intuition: The lookup table and output projection refer to the same Parameter, not two tables initialized with equal values. For vocabulary V and width D, this removes one V-by-D matrix relative to an independent bias-free output head.
takeaway: Gradients from both computational paths accumulate into that parameter. Sharing constrains the input and output representations to use one table; fewer parameters alone do not guarantee better quality.
reading: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models

title: Does top-k MoE select tokens or networks?
motivation: The same phrase, top-k, appears in both sampling and mixture-of-experts routing. They select completely different things.
intuition: For MoE, each token’s hidden state produces scores over expert networks. The router selects k experts, runs them, and combines their outputs. Sampling top-k instead restricts vocabulary candidates for the next token.
takeaway: Total parameters include all experts, while a token activates only some of them. Actual speed also depends on dispatch, load balance, and hardware utilization. Switch Transformers is useful sparse-routing background, although it uses top-1 routing rather than this project’s top-2 setup.
code: hidden state -> router -> selected experts -> weighted sum
